We need to propose a retrosynthesis route with 1 reaction (i.e., a single disconnection). The target SMILES: [CH2:1]=[C:2]([c:3]1[cH:4][cH:5][cH:6][cH:7][cH:8]1)[C@@H:9]1[CH2:10][CH2:11][CH2:12][C@@:13]1([OH:14])[C:15]([F:16])([F:17])[F:18]

Let's decode: It's a bicyclic? Actually it's a cyclopentane fused? Let's rewrite: There's an exocyclic alkene attached to a phenyl ring and to a chiral carbon that is part of a cyclopentane bearing OH and CF3. So the target is a cyclopentanol with CF3 attached, attached to an alkene that is conjugated to phenyl.

The guidance: carbonyl-ene reaction retrosynthesis: break a C-O bond (hydroxyl) and a C=C double bond to a carbonyl and an alkene. So forward reaction: carbonyl-ene forms a C-C bond, converting a carbonyl (ketone) and an alkene into an allylic alcohol (hydroxyl) and a new C-C bond, with loss of C=C. In retrosynthesis, we would disconnect the C-C bond formed, generating a ketone and an alkene.

Thus we need to propose a retrosynthetic step: target -> precursors: a ketone (probably a cyclopentanone with CF3) and an alkene (maybe styrene). The carbonyl-ene reaction would combine them to give the product.

Specifically, the product has a new C-C bond between the carbon bearing OH (C13) and the alkene carbon (C2). In the product, the OH is on C13 (attached to cyclopentane). In the forward carbonyl-ene, the carbonyl carbon becomes the carbon bearing OH? Actually in carbonyl-ene, the carbonyl oxygen becomes OH on the allylic position, and the carbonyl carbon becomes attached to the alkene carbon (forming new C-C). So the product's OH is on the carbon that was originally the carbonyl carbon? Wait typical carbonyl-ene: an alkene (ene) reacts with a carbonyl (enophile) to give an allylic alcohol. The carbonyl oxygen becomes OH on the allylic carbon (the carbon adjacent to the carbonyl carbon). The carbonyl carbon becomes attached to the alkene carbon (forming new sigma bond). So the product has an OH on the carbon that was originally the carbonyl carbon? Actually the allylic alcohol is formed at the carbon alpha to the carbonyl carbon. The carbonyl carbon becomes part of the new C-C bond. So the OH ends up on the carbon that was originally the carbonyl carbon? Let's recall: Example: acetone + isobutene under Lewis acid gives 4-methyl-3-penten-2-ol. The carbonyl carbon (C=O) becomes attached to the terminal carbon of the alkene, and the carbonyl oxygen becomes OH on the carbon alpha to carbonyl carbon (the original carbonyl carbon becomes a secondary alcohol?). Hmm.

Better to think: The ene reaction: C=C (ene) with allylic H, and a carbonyl (enophile). The product: new C-C bond between the alkene carbon (the one bearing the allylic H) and the carbonyl carbon, and the carbonyl oxygen becomes OH attached to the allylic carbon (the carbon that donated H). So the OH is on the allylic carbon (originally part of the alkene). So in our product, the OH is on the cyclopentane carbon (C13) which is part of the ring and attached to CF3. That carbon likely was the allylic carbon originally (part of alkene). The carbonyl carbon would be the other carbon (C9?) which is attached to phenyl and exocyclic double bond? Actually the product has an exocyclic double bond between C1= C2, where C2 is attached to phenyl and to C9 (the chiral carbon). So the new C-C bond is between C2 (alkene carbon) and C9 (the carbon bearing OH? Wait OH is on C13). Let's map: The SMILES: [CH2:1]=[C:2]([c:3]1... ) [C@@H:9]1[CH2:10][CH2:11][CH2:12][C@@:13]1([OH:14])[C:15]([F:16])([F:17])[F:18]

So C2 is attached to phenyl and to C9 (chiral). C9 is part of cyclopentane ring (C9 attached to C10). C13 is the carbon bearing OH and CF3 attached to C9? Actually C13 is the carbon opposite? The ring: C9- C10- C11- C12- C13 (closing to C9). C13 has OH and CF3 attached. So the OH is on C13, not C9. The new C-C bond formed in carbonyl-ene is between C2 (alkene carbon) and C9 (the carbonyl carbon). The OH appears on the allylic carbon which is C13? Wait the allylic carbon is the one adjacent to the carbonyl carbon in the enophile? In the carbonyl-ene, the allylic hydrogen is transferred from the alkene's allylic position to the carbonyl oxygen, forming OH on that allylic carbon. In our product, the OH is on C13, which is not directly adjacent to C9? In the cyclopentane, C9 is adjacent to C10 and C13 (since ring). So C13 is two bonds away? Actually ring: C9- C10- C11- C12- C13- back to C9. So C13 is adjacent to C9 (they are connected). So C13 is the allylic carbon relative to C9 (the carbonyl carbon). So that matches: C9 is carbonyl carbon (now attached to C2 and part of ring). C13 is allylic carbon bearing OH after reaction.

Thus retrosynthetic disconnection: break bond between C2 and C9, and break C-O bond (C13-OH) to give a carbonyl (C9=O) and an alkene (C2=CH2) with allylic hydrogen on C13? Actually the alkene is the same as product's alkene? The alkene in the starting material (ene) would be the same as the product's alkene? In carbonyl-ene, the alkene remains as double bond after reaction? No, the alkene is consumed; the double bond shifts? The product has a new double bond? Actually the product retains the alkene? In typical ene reaction, the alkene becomes a new sigma bond to carbonyl carbon, and the double bond moves to the allylic position? Wait typical ene: R-CH=CH2 (ene) + R'CHO (enophile) -> R-CH-CH2-CH(OH)-R' (allylic alcohol) where the double bond moves to between the original alkene carbon and the allylic carbon? Let's check example: Isobutene + acetone -> 4-methyl-3-penten-2-ol. Starting isobutene CH2=C(CH3)2, acetone (CH3COCH3). Product: CH3-CH2-C(OH)(CH3)-CH=CH2? Actually 4-methyl-3-penten-2-ol: CH3-CH2-C(OH)(CH3)-CH=CH2. So the double bond ends up between the carbon that was originally the terminal carbon of the alkene (CH2) and the carbon that was originally the carbonyl carbon? Hmm.

Given complexity, but we can propose a retrosynthetic step: target -> precursors: (1) cyclopentanone with CF3 at C13 (i.e., 3-(trifluoromethyl)cyclopentan-1-one?) Actually carbonyl at C9 (attached to phenyl and exocyclic alkene). The carbonyl carbon is attached to phenyl and to the cyclopentane ring. So the ketone would be phenyl-substituted cyclopentanone with CF3 at adjacent carbon? The other precursor is styrene (phenyl-CH=CH2). The carbonyl-ene would combine them.

Thus we need to find a template that matches carbonyl-ene transformation. Use search_template_catalog_by_criteria with functional_groups_broken: ['ketones'], functional_groups_formed: ['aliphatic hydroxyls'], bonds_broken: maybe ['6-6']? Not sure. Let's try search with functional_groups_broken list.
